kriyāpyarthasya kāyādestattaddeśādijātatā | nānyā'dṛṣṭerna sāpyekā kramikaikasya cocitā || 9 || saṃkṣepeṇa kārikārthamāha kriyā iti | adṛṣṭeḥ ityasya pramāṇena anupalabdherityayamartha iti darśayati pratyakṣa iti avasāyaparyantaḥ pramāṇavyāpāra iti dṛṣṭiravasāyaparyavasāyinī sūtre vyākhyeyā, yena anumānamapi sagrahīṣyate ityavaseyaśabdaḥ svarūpeṇa anyasaṃbandhitayā ceti pramāṇānavaseyatve yuktiṃbādhitve ca ubhayatrāpi saṃbandhanīyam | yuktyā pramāṇavyāpāreṇa bādhitatvaṃ svarūpata uktam na sāpyekā kramikā iti, anyasaṃbandhitayā tu uktam ekasya kramikā kathaṃ bhavet iti | ātmana aiśvaryaṃ jñānakriyāyogādityevaṃrūpaparodīryamāṇahetudūṣaṇaprakaṭa- nalabdhaṃ yat punaḥ sūtradvaye prasaṅgāpādanābhidhāyini prasaṅgaviparyaye viśrāntyā tasmāt jñānaṃ na yuktamiti jñānasya ayuktatvaṃ, tat kriyāyāmiha sūtre vṛttau ca apiśabdena samuccīyate,-ityāśayena vivṛṇoti na kevalam iti | anena ca kriyāpi na yuktā iti vṛttirvyākhyātā | pūrvasūtravṛttau sadapi iti apiśabdasya artho vyākhyātaḥ, etatsūtragatasya tu ayamarthaḥ ityāha atrāpi ityapiśabdena ṭīkākāraḥ | evaṃ ca vadan sūtravṛttyorekagranthatāṃ sphuṭayati | tatra iti na yukteti vaktavye satītyarthaḥ; yadivā tatreti ātmani kriyā | sā tāvat laukikī calanarūpā karmapadārthatvena padārthavidbhirupagatā na bhavati ātmano mūrtihīnasya mūrtyanuvidhāyinī sā nopagatā yataḥ | tairhi ātmano jñānacikīrṣāyatnayoge eva kartṛtvaṃ prasādhitaṃ, jñānādayaśca (page 184) guṇāśca tatsamavāyaśca na kriyeti tādṛśī kriyā vaktavyā, yā ātmanaḥ saṃbhāvyate | tadāha iti lakṣaṇam | kārakasya phalasiddhihetubhūtakriyāni- mittasya svakriyāpekṣayā vākartuḥ saṃbandhī tatsamavāyī tadātmā vā vyāpāro rūpaṃ svaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ yasyāḥ, sā kriyā yasyāḥ saṃbandhino bhāgāḥ pūrvāparībhūtāḥ kramavṛttayaḥ iti yāvat | yadāha tatrabhavān yāvatsiddhamasiddhaṃ vā sādhyatvenābhidhīyate | āśritakramarūpatvāttatkriyeti pratīyate || guṇabhūtairavayavaiḥ samūhaḥ kramajanmanām | buddhyā prakalpitābhedaḥ kriyeti vyapadiśyate || śvetaṃ
**Action is the ordered operation, not a thing that moves** The opponent had offered the self's lordship as the union of knowledge and action. We have seen that knowledge cannot be a separate thing in his view. Now Abhinavagupta shows that *action* cannot be a separate thing either. Kārikā 9 makes the point: the action of a body is just the coming-to-be of this or that place; it is not some hidden cause (the unseen, adṛṣṭa) moving it; and it is not one — for order does not belong to a single thing. But wait — if action is not a movement, what is it? The word-knowers, the grammarians, refuse to say that the body-less self moves. They locate the self's agency only in the union of knowledge, desire, and effort. So the action that belongs to the self must be defined differently. Its marker, Abhinavagupta says, is this: the operation of the agent that brings about the fruit — the means, related to the doer, or inhering in it, or its very self — whose form is such that its parts are prior-and-later, standing in order. Action is the ordered operation. And the gurus' verses make this vivid: "as long as the established or un-established is spoken of as the to-be-established, being of the resting-order-form, it is perceived as that action." The mass of order-born parts, unified by the mind, is what we call action. "White is whitened" — the whiteness appears as a prior-later order, and that is the declaration of action. So action is not a thing that moves; it is the ordered self-shaping of a nature. And this action is in the self. "He desires, he knows, he strives" — these are the prior-later dharmas of the one self, perceived in their order; and this ordered operation, Abhinavagupta notes, is accepted by the very thinkers who hold the self to be the Lord. The guru's words: "such is the will, such the knowledge, such the action." The will, the knowledge, the action — these are not three separate things attached to a self; they are the one self's ordered operation, its desiring and knowing and striving, held together as the single action. So the action, like the cognition, cannot be broken into momentary flashes or hidden causes. It is the one, ordered operation of the self — the will that knows and acts. And this is why the union of knowledge and action is not a reason that the opponent can offer for lordship; it is the self's own nature. The self that desires, knows, and strives — in that single ordered act — is the Lord. The union of knowledge and action is not a quality added to the self; it is the self, shining as the ordered operation of the one who wills and knows and does. ---

> Having shown the cognition is impossible in the opponent's view, Abhinavagupta now shows action > (kriyā) is impossible too. Kārikā 9: the action of a body is the coming-to-be of this and that > place-and-the-rest; it is not other, from the unseen (adṛṣṭa); nor is it one — for the ordered (the > sequence) of the one is not fit. One action cannot be at once this place and that; a single action > could not produce the ordered succession.
